# Personal Statement

Economics has always interested me because of how it explain human behavior and society. During my junior year at State University, I took Professor Chen's Intermediate Microeconomics course, which was a turning point for me, it really showed me how powerful economic models could be when applied to real problems. I became fascinated with behavioral economics after reading Thaler's work on mental accounting, and I decided to write my senior thesis on how loss aversion affects consumer spending decisions during recessions. I conducted surveys of 300 households in the Columbus area and analyzed their purchasing patterns using regression analysis. The data showed that households with higher loss aversion scores were significantly less likely to make discretionary purchases even after the recession had ended, suggesting that psychological factors can have persistent economic effects. I also worked at the Columbus Metropolitan Planning Organization last summer as an intern, where I helped analyze transportation infrastructure data and prepared reports on how different zoning policies effect property values and commuting patterns. This work was rewarding because I could see economists' theories actually being used in practice to make decisions that affected real communities.

Beyond coursework and internships, my commitment to understanding economics deepens through several extracurricular activities. I was president of the Economics Club for two years, organizing guest speakers from local firms and coordinating a case competition where students applied economic principles to business strategy problems. I also volunteer as a tutor for intro economics at the community college, which have taught me how to explain complicated concepts in accessible ways. Graduate school in economics represents the natural next step in my academic journey, and I am particularly interested in behavioral economics and urban economics, which is why your program's emphasis on applied microeconomics appeals to me greatly. I believe that a master's degree will give me the tools and training to conduct meaningful research on how people make decisions and how policy can be designed more effectively.

# Personal Statement

What draws me to graduate study in economics is a specific puzzle: how psychological factors like loss aversion interact with features of the built environment—zoning, housing markets, transportation access—to shape household spending decisions long after the immediate shock of a recession has passed. This question first took shape during my junior year at State University, in Professor Chen's Intermediate Microeconomics course; that course revealed the predictive precision of economic models when applied to real-world behavior. After reading Thaler's work on mental accounting, I became fascinated with behavioral economics and decided to write my senior thesis on how loss aversion affects consumer spending decisions during recessions. I conducted surveys of 300 households in the Columbus area and analyzed their purchasing patterns using regression analysis. What the thesis could not tell me, however, was whether these effects varied by neighborhood characteristics—whether households in areas with different housing stability or commuting burdens experienced loss aversion differently. That open question is what I want to pursue in graduate school.

My internship at the Columbus Metropolitan Planning Organization last summer sharpened this interest further. There, I analyzed transportation infrastructure data and prepared reports on how different zoning policies affect property values and commuting patterns. This work was rewarding because I could see economic theory being used to make decisions that affected real communities, and it convinced me that the intersection of behavioral and urban economics—how psychological biases operate within specific spatial and policy contexts—is where I want to build my research. This is why your program's emphasis on applied microeconomics, and particularly Professor Alvarez's research on housing markets and consumer decision-making, matters to me: I want the methodological training to test whether loss aversion operates differently across neighborhoods with different zoning histories, using the kind of applied microeconomic tools your program emphasizes.

My commitment to this direction extends beyond coursework and internships. As president of the Economics Club for two years, I organized guest speakers from local firms and coordinated a case competition applying economic principles to business strategy. I also tutor introductory economics at the community college, which has taught me that the psychological barriers students face in understanding new concepts often parallel the psychological barriers to rational decision-making I study in my research—both require close attention to how people process information under uncertainty. Graduate school represents the training I need to pursue these questions rigorously. I believe a master's degree will equip me to conduct research on how loss aversion and other psychological biases interact with local housing and labor market conditions, and how policy might be designed to account for these effects.

# Personal Statement

During my sophomore year, I noticed that my roommate kept buying the same brand of coffee even after prices rose sharply and cheaper alternatives appeared on the shelf—a small, ordinary decision that nonetheless seemed to defy the rational-actor models I had just learned in introductory economics. That contradiction stayed with me, and when I took Professor Chen's Intermediate Microeconomics course during my junior year at State University, it became a turning point: the course showed me how powerful economic models could be when applied to real problems, but it also left me curious about where those models broke down. I became fascinated with behavioral economics after reading Thaler's work on mental accounting, and I decided to write my senior thesis on how loss aversion affects consumer spending decisions during recessions.

I conducted surveys of 300 households in the Columbus area and analyzed their purchasing patterns using regression analysis. The data showed that households with higher loss aversion scores were significantly less likely to make discretionary purchases even after the recession had ended, suggesting that psychological factors can have persistent economic effects. What surprised me most was that this effect persisted even among households whose income had fully recovered, which challenged my initial assumption that loss aversion was primarily a response to ongoing financial constraint rather than a lingering psychological habit. That finding pushed me to start thinking about loss aversion not as a temporary bias but as something that might interact with place-based factors—housing costs, local labor markets—in ways standard models don't capture, which is part of what draws me to urban economics as well.

I also worked at the Columbus Metropolitan Planning Organization last summer as an intern, where I helped analyze transportation infrastructure data and prepared reports on how different zoning policies affect property values and commuting patterns. The experience complicated my understanding of applied economics more than it confirmed it: in one case, a proposed rezoning that theory predicted would raise nearby property values instead met fierce resident opposition rooted in concerns the models simply didn't account for, and the final policy reflected a compromise that no regression could have predicted. That taught me that translating economic theory into policy requires grappling with political and social constraints that aren't always visible in the data—a lesson I want to carry into graduate research.

These research and internship experiences also shaped how I approached my extracurricular involvement. As president of the Economics Club for two years, I organized guest speakers from local firms and coordinated a case competition where students applied economic principles to business strategy problems; preparing students to defend their models under questioning sharpened my own ability to articulate the assumptions behind economic reasoning. Tutoring introductory economics at the community college has pushed this further: explaining concepts like opportunity cost or elasticity to students encountering them for the first time has forced me to identify exactly where intuition and formal theory diverge, which has sharpened my own thinking about behavioral economics far more than passively studying it would have.

Graduate school represents the next step in pursuing the question that has run through all of this work: how psychological factors like loss aversion interact with place-specific conditions to shape economic behavior in ways that matter for policy. Your program's emphasis on applied microeconomics, combined with faculty research connecting behavioral insights to housing and labor markets, is precisely the environment where I could pursue this question rigorously. I am particularly interested in extending the survey methodology from my thesis to examine how loss aversion shapes housing decisions across different metropolitan areas, a project that would build directly on both my research background and my firsthand exposure to zoning and property-value data at the MPO. I believe my combination of hands-on survey research, practical policy experience, and sustained work explaining economic ideas to others positions me to contribute meaningfully to your program from day one.

What surprised me most was how long this effect lingered: even households whose income had fully recovered continued to spend conservatively months later. # Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Your personal statement demonstrates genuine intellectual engagement with economics and provides solid evidence of your commitment to the field through coursework, research, and practical experience. However, there are several areas where revision would strengthen your application significantly.

**Grammar and Mechanics**

Start by addressing the grammatical errors that distract from your message. In your opening sentence, "how it explain" should be "how it explains." In the first paragraph, you have a comma splice: "which was a turning point for me, it really showed me" needs either a semicolon, a period, or a subordinating conjunction to connect these clauses properly. Later, you write that zoning policies "effect property values" when you mean "affect"—effect is primarily a noun, while affect is the verb you need here. In your second paragraph, "volunteer as a tutor for intro economics at the community college, which have taught me" contains a subject-verb agreement error; "which" is singular, so it should be "has taught me." These errors, while individually small, accumulate and suggest less careful attention to your writing than graduate admissions committees expect.

**Word Choice and Clarity**

Beyond mechanical errors, some of your word choices could be more precise. In the opening, you say economics interests you "because of how it explain human behavior and society," but this phrasing is somewhat vague. What specific aspects of human behavior? What scale of society are you discussing? Being more concrete here would immediately establish you as a thoughtful analyst rather than someone making a general statement. Later, you write that you "became fascinated" with behavioral economics after reading Thaler—while enthusiasm is good, the word "fascinated" is somewhat informal for an academic context and doesn't tell us what specifically compelled you intellectually. Did his framework change how you understood a problem? Did it challenge an assumption you held?

**Paragraph Structure and Development**

Your first paragraph tries to do too much. It begins with a general interest statement, introduces a formative course, pivots to behavioral economics and your senior thesis, describes your methodology and findings, then shifts again to your internship. While all of this content is relevant, the paragraph lacks a clear through-line. Consider whether your senior thesis and your internship work toward a single coherent narrative. Right now, they feel like separate accomplishments being listed rather than parts of a developing intellectual project. The reader should understand how your thesis work on loss aversion and your internship on zoning policy and property values connect—or if they don't connect, why you're including both.

Your second paragraph has its own organizational challenge. You move from extracurricular activities to your tutoring experience to your future goals all in quick succession. The extracurricular activities (Economics Club leadership and case competition) deserve more explanation about what you learned from them. You mention organizing guest speakers and coordinating competitions, but not what impact these had on your thinking or development. Similarly, your tutoring experience gets only a single clause of explanation before you pivot to your graduate aspirations. This paragraph would benefit from either expansion—giving each activity more weight—or condensation—focusing on fewer activities in greater depth.

**Achieving Your Purpose**

Personal statements succeed when they help admissions committees understand not just what you've done, but who you are as a thinker and scholar. Your statement effectively documents your activities, but it sometimes tells rather than shows. For instance, you conclude by saying a master's degree will give you "tools and training to conduct meaningful research," but you haven't fully conveyed what makes the research meaningful to you or what specific questions drive your intellectual curiosity. Your senior thesis findings about persistent loss aversion effects are interesting—why do you think understanding this matters? What problem does it solve? The internship work on zoning policy is practical and grounded—but what did you discover about the relationship between economic theory and policy implementation that surprised or troubled you?

The strongest personal statements reveal the applicant's intellectual character—what they wonder about, what frustrates them, what they're driven to understand. Instead of saying you're "interested in" behavioral and urban economics, show us a question or tension in the field that genuinely compels you. You have several subject-verb agreement errors that need attention. In your first paragraph, you write "which are causing algal blooms that is devastating the ecosystem"—here "blooms" (plural) takes "are," but "is" should be "are." Later, you write "understanding the science behind environmental problems are just as important," but the subject "understanding" is singular and needs "is." In the same section, "learning about eutrophication in the classroom while I were collecting data" should use "was" instead of "were." These errors are easy to fix with careful proofreading, but they do weaken an otherwise polished statement.

**Word Choice and Tone**

Watch for moments where your language becomes slightly informal or imprecise for an academic context. The phrase "I got really interested in understanding why" feels conversational; consider "I became interested in investigating" or simply "I became interested in understanding." Similarly, "doesn't just publish papers but actually helps communities" uses "actually" in a way that can feel dismissive of pure research—you might say "not only publishes papers but also helps communities" to avoid implying that research alone is less valuable. These small shifts will make your voice sound more measured and professional.

**Structure and Development**

Your two paragraphs follow a logical progression: first establishing your foundational interest in water quality, then narrowing to your specific graduate focus on agricultural runoff and soil science. This is effective. However, the first paragraph tries to accomplish quite a bit—it moves from your volunteer experience to a classroom experience to your club work to your research presentation. While these are all relevant, the paragraph feels slightly rushed. You might consider whether every detail serves your argument. For instance, the Mid-Atlantic Undergraduate Research Conference could be mentioned more briefly, or you could select one or two of your most significant involvements rather than listing them all.

**Specificity and Evidence**

Generally, your use of specific details is a strength. You name actual places (Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Potomac River, Patuxent River watershed), people (Dr. Patricia Chen), and scientific concepts (eutrophication, macroinvertebrates, cover crops). This grounds your statement in reality. For a graduate school application, admissions committees want to understand not just what you've done, but why you're ready for graduate-level work and why you're a good fit for their program. This statement successfully conveys your passion, your hands-on experience, and your intellectual maturity. # Personal Statement

My interest in art history developed gradually during my undergraduate years, though it wasn't until my junior year that I really committed myself to the field seriously. While taking Professor Martinez's seminar on Italian Renaissance portraiture, I became fascinated by how artists like Botticelli and Leonardo used visual language to communicate ideas about power and identity, which I had never considered before. This class was pivotal because it taught me how to look at paintings in a more rigorous way, analyzing composition and iconography rather than just aesthetic pleasure. I also did an internship at the Blanton Museum where I catalogued works from their Latin American collection, and this experience was really important for my career goals because I learned how museums actually function behind the scenes, working with provenance research and conservation reports. What I found most rewarding was assisting with an exhibition on Diego Rivera's political murals, preparing wall texts and interviewing local artists who was influenced by his work. Beyond coursework and internships, I have always been drawn to how art reflects the societies that produced it, which led me to write my senior thesis on Mexican retablos and their role in folk spirituality during the colonial period. These experiences has shaped my understanding of art history as a discipline that is relevant and urgent in today's world.

My goal in pursuing graduate study is to deepen my knowledge of visual culture in Latin America and to eventually work in museum curation or academia. I believe that a strong graduate program will equip me with the theoretical frameworks and archival skills necessary for conducting original research. The rigor I encountered in my thesis work, examining primary sources at the Harry Ransom Center, have prepared me for graduate-level thinking. I am particularly interested in studying under faculty who specialize in colonial and modern Latin American art, as I have found this field offers rich opportunities for interrogating questions about cultural identity, diaspora, and resistance. Moving forward into graduate school, I'm excited to contribute my passion for this region's artistic traditions while also developing more sophisticated methodologies for interpreting visual meaning and understanding how museums can be spaces for cultural dialogue and change.

Let’s start with purpose, since that matters most in a document meant to persuade an admissions committee. Right now the statement reads as a competent summary of your undergraduate experiences rather than an argument for why you, specifically, should be admitted to a particular graduate program. Admissions readers see dozens of statements that list a meaningful class, an internship, and a thesis; what will distinguish yours is the throughline connecting these experiences to a specific scholarly question you want to pursue and to what a graduate program can offer that you cannot get on your own. Without this, the statement could be sent to any art history program with only minor edits, which readers will notice.

On structure, the first paragraph tries to do too much by moving chronologically through every major experience (seminar, internship, thesis) in list-like fashion, with each new experience introduced by "I also did" or "Beyond coursework." This creates a catalog rather than a narrative arc. Consider instead organizing the paragraph around an idea, using your experiences as evidence rather than as a chronological inventory. For example, you might frame the paragraph around the development of your analytical method: how the Martinez seminar taught you to read images rigorously, how the Blanton internship taught you to think about the institutional and material lives of objects, and how the thesis let you apply both to original research. That reframing would let you cut some of the more mechanical transitions and instead build toward a clear closing claim in that paragraph about what those experiences taught you collectively, rather than the fairly generic claim you currently end on ("art history as a discipline that is relevant and urgent in today's world"), which needs to be either sharpened with a concrete example or cut.

The second paragraph is more focused, but it also tends to stay at the level of generality. Phrases like "theoretical frameworks and archival skills necessary for conducting original research" or "developing more sophisticated methodologies for interpreting visual meaning" sound like the kind of thing any applicant could write. Try to replace at least one or two of these general statements with something concrete: a specific methodology you want to learn (for instance, a particular theoretical approach to visual culture, or a specific archival or digital humanities skill), or a specific way you imagine using it in your future research or curatorial work.

Now to some sentence-level issues. A customer had abandoned a purchase because a search query took twelve seconds to return results. That gap between a line of inefficient code and a real person's frustration was the moment I understood, viscerally, what "performance" actually means. It isn't an abstraction measured in milliseconds; it's the difference between someone trusting a system and someone walking away from it. That realization has shaped nearly everything I've chosen to study since.

I spent the rest of that summer chasing the source of delays like that one, eventually restructuring queries and rebuilding indexes across Clearwater's customer management system until response times dropped by 38%. But the more interesting discovery wasn't the number itself—it was how much of the slowness lived in decisions made years earlier, when the system was small enough that inefficiency didn't matter. Watching a legacy architecture strain under growth taught me that performance isn't a fixed achievement; it's a moving target that shifts as scale changes the rules. That tension is what pulled me toward distributed systems: I wanted to understand how you design for growth you can't yet see.

I'd been circling that kind of problem long before I had language for it. In high school, three years with FIRST Robotics meant spending competition nights debugging a system while five teammates argued over which sensor was lying to us. What I took from those nights wasn't just comfort with troubleshooting under pressure—it was learning to listen for the quiet assumption buried in a design that turns out to be wrong once conditions change. That instinct is exactly what resurfaced when I stared at Clearwater's legacy queries: the code wasn't broken, it was just built for a world that no longer existed.

That's the question I want to spend graduate school pursuing: how do you build systems that stay fast and correct as the assumptions underneath them keep shifting? Distributed databases make this question especially hard, since consistency and speed pull against each other the moment you spread data across machines. I want to work on query optimization techniques for exactly this kind of environment, and I've started teaching myself by contributing small patches to PostgreSQL, trying to understand its optimizer from the inside rather than just as a user of it. My coursework in systems and databases has given me a foundation, but it's this outside tinkering—reading through real optimizer code and seeing where my intuitions break—that has convinced me I want to do this as research, not just as engineering.

Your program's reputation in distributed systems is part of what draws me, but it was reading Professor Chen's work on distributed transaction processing that made the fit feel concrete: her approach to reasoning about consistency guarantees under failure is close to the kind of problem I keep returning to on my own. I don't yet have a polished answer to the question that's been forming since that twelve-second query—I have a habit of noticing when a system's assumptions have quietly stopped matching reality, and the persistence to go find out why. That's what I hope to bring to your department.

In your first paragraph, "this experience were transformative" should be "this experience was transformative" since "experience" is singular. Similarly, "I seen firsthand" should be "I saw firsthand"—the past participle "seen" requires an auxiliary verb. Later, "social determinants...was preventing" should use "were" because the subject is plural. These errors appear repeatedly throughout ("my passion...have only grown" should be "has only grown"; "which were exciting" should be "was exciting"; "community members' concerns...was not always being heard" should be "were not always being heard"). You also have punctuation and apostrophe errors that need attention. "Public health require's us" should not have an apostrophe—this is a straightforward plural verb, not a possessive. A single transitional sentence at the start of paragraph two (something like "This recognition that health is shaped by one's environment carried into my next experience...") would make the statement feel like a unified argument rather than two separate stories stapled together.

Within paragraph one, watch for redundancy.
